st: Peel the breadfruit with a sharp knife, cut it into quarters, and cut out the tough core. Slice the flesh into 1.5-inch chunks.
Put the breadfruit chunks in a medium pot with [[1 cup]] water and [[0.5 tsp]] salt. Bring to a boil over high heat.
Lower the heat, cover, and simmer for 15 minutes until the breadfruit is just starting to soften.
Stir in the sliced onion, [[2 cups]] coconut milk, [[1 tbsp]] sugar, and the remaining [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Keep the pot at a gentle simmer, partly covered, and stir carefully every few minutes so the chunks do not break up.
Taste the sauce and add a little more salt if needed. The breadfruit should be tender and the sauce creamy.
Let it rest for 5 minutes off the heat so the sauce thickens, then serve warm as a side.

ing: whole, live or fresh cooked large crabs or crab legs
st: If your crab is uncooked, ask the fishmonger to humanely prepare it, or use fresh crab legs. Rinse well under cold water.
Bring [[2 l]] water to a boil in a very large pot and stir in [[1 tbsp]] salt.
Add the crab and boil for 20 minutes, until the shell is bright orange-red and the meat is opaque and firm.
Meanwhile, simmer [[1.5 cups]] coconut milk with [[5 cloves]] minced garlic and [[0.5 tsp]] black pepper in a small pan over low heat for 8 minutes.
Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the juice of the limes.
Lift the crab out with tongs and let it drain for a few minutes. Crack the shell with a mallet or the back of a heavy knife.
Pour the warm garlic coconut sauce over the cracked crab or serve it in bowls for dipping. Add lime wedges at the table.

ing: seeded and minced, or to taste
st: Buy tuna labeled safe to eat raw and keep it very cold until you use it. Cut it into 0.5-inch cubes with a sharp knife.
Put the tuna in a glass or ceramic bowl, not metal. Pour over the juice of [[5 limes]] and add [[0.5 tsp]] salt.
Stir gently, cover, and refrigerate for 15 minutes. The fish will turn opaque on the outside as the lime cures it.
Meanwhile, finely dice the onion, mince the chili, and dice the cucumber if using.
Drain off about half of the lime juice from the fish.
Stir in the onion, chili, and cucumber, then pour in [[0.5 cup]] chilled coconut milk.
Taste, add salt or more chili if you like, and serve right away, very cold.
Wear gloves if you have them, since raw taro can irritate skin. Peel the taro and cut it into 1.5-inch chunks.
Put the taro in a pot with [[2 cups]] water and [[0.25 tsp]] salt. Bring to a boil.
Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 20 minutes until a knife slides in easily.
Drain off most of the water, leaving about 3 tablespoons in the pot.
Add the sliced onion, [[1.5 cups]] coconut milk, [[1 tbsp]] sugar, and the remaining [[0.25 tsp]] salt.
Simmer gently, uncovered, for 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and creamy.
Taste, adjust the salt, and serve warm. Never eat taro undercooked.

ing: snapper or similar, scaled and gutted
st: Rinse the fish and pat it dry. Cut three diagonal slashes into each side so the heat can reach the thickest part.
Mix the juice of the limes, [[2 tbsp]] soy sauce, [[1 tbsp]] oil, [[3 cloves]] minced garlic, [[0.5 tsp]] salt, and [[0.5 tsp]] pepper in a small bowl.
Rub the mixture over the fish and into the slashes. Let it marinate for 15 minutes.
Heat a charcoal grill or gas grill to medium-high. Clean the grate and brush it with the remaining [[1 tbsp]] oil.
Grill the fish for 6 minutes without moving it so it releases cleanly.
Flip carefully with a wide spatula and grill 5 to 6 minutes more, until the flesh flakes easily and reaches 145°F (63°C).
Rest the fish for 3 minutes and serve with extra lime.
